chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.note: Not a proper kephalaion but a framing/justification sequence for the entire work. The oldest teaching layer survives as a compressed cosmogonic survey in paragraphs 1-9, mapping the full cosmic drama from primordial separation through final reintegration. Both sides of every mapping stay within the cosmic system — realm structures, cosmic agents, cosmic processes. Heavy lacunae throughout. Paragraphs 10-23 are entirely institutional: Mani asserting scriptural authority, narrating earlier apostles (Jesus, Zarathustra, Buddha), and commanding disciples to preserve his oral teaching — the editorial justification for compiling the Kephalaia. Editorial fatigue is strong (0.67), with substrate vocabulary disappearing completely in the second half while institutional vocabulary doubles. The cosmogonic substrate is genuine but presented in highly compressed summary form, likely an editorial condensation of fuller substrate teaching found in later chapters.

chapters.title: Concerning the Ad[vent] of the Apostle
chapters.note: This chapter is entirely institutional/apostolic narrative with no extractable substrate. Teaching purity is near zero (0.018). The chapter traces apostolic succession from Sethel through Jesus to Mani, recounts Mani's autobiography (calling, revelation by the Paraclete, missionary journeys), and frames his apostolate as the fulfillment of Jesus's Paraclete promise. The agricultural metaphor (farmer/harvest/Parmuthi-Paophi) maps apostles→farmers and churches→harvest seasons — both sides of the mapping are institutional/worldly, not cosmological. Cosmological content appears only as referenced topics in the revelation summary (¶24-25: 'the mystery of the light and the darkness,' ships, Adam) but is never actually taught — it functions as a table of contents for cosmological teachings given elsewhere. NT citations (Phil. 2:7 servant's form, John 14-16 Paraclete passages) confirm the editorial period. The chapter is bookended by dialogue frame conventions (opening question ¶1-2, formulaic closing ¶31). This is a foundational institutional text for the Manichaean community, establishing Mani's legitimacy through apostolic succession.

chapters.title: The Second, concerning the Parable of the Tree.
chapters.note: This chapter is heavily overlaid with editorial material. The first half (¶1-11) is almost entirely dialogue frame, Gospel citation, and anti-sectarian polemic — the editors use Jesus' parable as a proof-text and argue against 'the sects' using NT examples (Judas, Paul, the date palm). The substrate teaching emerges in the second half with the five-fold faculty mapping: consideration, counsel, insight, thought, mind → cosmic beings/locations for both the good tree (ascending: holy church → Pillar of Glory → First Man → Third Ambassador → the Father) and the bad tree (descending: law of death → transmigration → gehenna → vessel → the lump). This systematic faculty-realm correspondence is the oldest layer. The chapter closes with a dualistic creedal assertion (the two trees did not arise from one another) wrapped in exhortation. The editorial fatigue pattern is confirmed: substrate vocabulary increases in the second half while frame/institutional vocabulary drifts upward. The 'taste' mappings (good tree → holy church/catechumens; bad tree → the sects) are editorial applications that reach outside the cosmic system into contemporary institutions.

chapters.title: The Interpretation of Happiness, Wisdom and Power; what they signify.
chapters.note: The oldest teaching layer is a four-fold descending iteration mapping happiness, wisdom, and power to cosmic beings at four levels: (1) the Father/land of light, (2) the sun ship, (3) the moon ship, (4) the elements. Each iteration follows the same triadic structure (happiness=sovereign being, wisdom=cognitive/generative being, power=the gods/angels at that level). This is pure cosmos→cosmos mapping. An editor extended this to a fifth level (the holy church, ¶9) by mimicking the pattern syntax — detected by bridge connective 'Now, moreover' and institutional vocabulary. The chapter's editorial fatigue score confirms significant institutional drift in the second half (+4.77). The summary in ¶10 integrates the editorial extension ('five churches') and closes with a beatitude. Paragraphs 1-4 are frame/setup with the topic question in ¶2 being substantive.

chapters.title: Concerning the Four Great Days that have come forth from one another, together with the Four Nights
chapters.note: The oldest teaching layer is dominant. A four-fold day/night schema maps cosmic entities to twelve-hour structures. The substrate is clean through the first three positions of each sequence. The fourth positions (day 4 = Jesus the Splendour, night 4 = law of Sin) show editorial bridging toward institutional identifications ('his church,' 'the twelve sects,' 'the old man'). This is a classic pattern: the editor extends a complete cosmic schema into the contemporary world at the terminal position. The substrate pentadic structure (five elements, five sense organs, five spirits) underlies the twelve-fold systematization, which Gardner rightly notes is 'secondary' — yet the cosmic correspondences within each position (zodiacal signs as Matter's thrones, five parts above/below, heat and cold as father and mother) are genuinely substratic. Editorial fatigue is moderate: substrate vocabulary drops from 34.09 to 8.62 in the second half while editorial_bridge rises from 0.0 to 2.39.

chapters.title: Concerning Four Hunters of Light and Four of Darkness
chapters.note: The substrate is a well-preserved four-fold parallel enumeration mapping cosmic agents to hunter correspondences (net, ship, sea). Both light and dark series follow the same structural template. The substrate is dominant in the light hunters (except P4 where 'his holy church' intrudes) and in the first three dark hunters. The fourth dark hunter (P11) is almost entirely overwritten by editorial bridge material identifying 'every sect' and 'erroneous teaching' in the contemporary world. Two exhortation beatitudes close each series. The substrate vocabulary drops sharply in the second half, consistent with editorial fatigue replacing the fourth dark hunter's cosmic content with polemical application.

chapters.title: Concerning the Five Storehouses that have poured forth from the Land of Darkness since the [Beginning]; the Five Rulers, the Five Spirits, the Five Bodies, the Five Tastes.
chapters.note: The oldest teaching layer is dominant in the first two-thirds of this chapter: a systematic five-fold cosmological description of the Kingdom of Darkness, mapping storehouses→elements→trees→genera→worlds, then describing the King of Darkness through zoomorphic forms (lion/eagle/dragon/fish), five properties (darkness/putridity/ugliness/bitterness/burning), three faculties (hardness/magic arts/polyglot knowledge), and further properties (movement/terrifying voice/perceptual limitation). The five sub-king descriptions (¶12-16) each contain pristine substrate (zoomorphic face + metal correspondence + taste correspondence) followed by editorial bridge material applying the cosmic spirit to contemporary institutions ('reigns today in the principalities,' 'sects that worship fire,' 'sites of idols,' 'baptism of the waters,' 'soothsayers'). The editorial fatigue pattern is textbook: +10.29 editorial_bridge drift in the second half. Gardner notes textual development and redactorial confusion about the King of Darkness vs. King of Smoke hierarchy. The substrate's five-fold degree structure (Smoke/Fire/Wind/Water/Darkness → gold/copper/iron/silver/lead → salty/sour/sharp/sweet/bitter → lion/eagle/fish/dragon) is a quintessential correspondential map with both sides internal to the cosmic system.

chapters.title: The Seventh, concerning the Five Fathers
chapters.note: A well-preserved emanation hierarchy teaching: five fathers, each summoning three powers. The substrate is dominant in ¶2-12, forming a clean systematic sequence. Editorial fatigue is clearly visible from ¶13 onward, where the editors increasingly overlay institutional vocabulary (churches, elect, catechumens) onto the emanation scheme. The substrate identifications survive even in the second half, but the functional descriptions shift from cosmos→cosmos to cosmos→institution. The emanation pattern language ('after the pattern of') is structural substrate. A gospel citation (John 8:38) intrudes at ¶15. The chapter closes with a standard beatitude formula.

chapters.title: Concerning the Fourteen Vehicles that Jesus has boarded
chapters.note: Clear two-part structure: paragraphs 2-8 contain a systematic ten-vehicle cosmic descent teaching (the substrate core), while paragraphs 9-10 are later editorial additions extending the pattern to institutional content and closing with a beatitude. The ten vehicles map a coherent cosmological descent sequence: from the light ship and Ambassador, through the ship of the First Man and Pillar of Glory, through the Call and Answer (summons/obedience), and finally through the five light elements (air, wind, light, water, fire). Gardner notes this reverses the ascent order familiar from Ch. 71, confirming its systematic character. The editorial seam at paragraph 9 is textbook: 'After he had assumed these ten, he came and manifested in the flesh. He chose the holy church in four vehicles.' — the editor mimics the enumeration pattern but applies it to Manichaean community categories. Editorial fatigue data strongly supports this division.

chapters.title: The Explanation of the Peace, what it is; the Right Hand; the Kiss; the Salutation.
chapters.note: This chapter presents the five ritual signs (peace, right hand, kiss, salutation, laying on of hands) as cosmic archetypes established by the First Man's descent to battle and ascent from victory. The oldest teaching layer is a two-series cosmological narrative: Series 1 (descent, ¶3–9) is nearly pure substrate; Series 2 (ascent, ¶10–14) preserves substrate cosmic narrative overlaid with editorial bridge formulas ('appropriate to the mystery of X, this Y has come about among mankind'). Significant editorial fatigue confirmed: substrate drops from 6.68→2.02 while institutional rises 2.18→9.16 in the second half. The chapter transitions from pure cosmic teaching through mixed cosmic+bridge to fully institutional application (¶16–19) and exhortation (¶21–24). A Light Form/Daēnā passage (¶20) preserves genuinely ancient Persian imagery of the soul's cosmic encounter. The Psalm 110:1 citation in ¶14 is a clear editorial insertion within cosmic narrative. The five-fold enumeration structure (peace, right hand, kiss, salutation, laying on of hands) is the substrate's organizational spine.

chapters.title: Concerning the Interpretation of the Fourteen [Great Aeons] of Light, about which Sethel has spoken in [his Prayer]

The final paragraph, though heavily lacunose, contains significant cosmological description of the Ambassador's role. The negative editorial fatigue score reflects the frame-heavy opening giving way to denser teaching in the second half.

Negative editorial fatigue (-1.08) confirms the substrate holds through the chapter with minimal drift.

chapters.title: [Concerning the Five] Greatnesses who [went forth] against the Darkness.
chapters.note: The oldest teaching layer is overwhelmingly dominant. The similes use natural correspondences (noble son, judge, king inspecting craftsmen, fig-garden, butter in milk) to map cosmic processes — classic correspondential teaching method where both sides stay within the system. Only the opening dialogue formula (¶1) and closing beatitude (¶30) are clearly later layers. The 'Now, just as' formulas in ¶15 and ¶21 are simile-completion structures integral to the teaching, not editorial seams — they map analogy→cosmic entity with no institutional content. Gardner's note that Jesus the Splendour as fifth greatness 'may be a later development' is worth noting but at the textual level ¶7 follows the same enumeration pattern as ¶2-6.

chapters.title: Concerning the Light Mind and the Apostles and the Saints
chapters.note: Long, complex chapter with a dominant substrate layer centered on body-cosmos correspondence (macro-micro mapping). Core substrate teaching includes: (1) the universe constructed as a human body (¶11-12) — classic correspondential mapping of organs to cosmic structures; (2) five sons of the Living Spirit as five intellectual faculties stationed in five cosmic watch-districts (¶13-17); (3) rebellion narratives in each watch-district with cosmic responses (¶19-28); (4) the soul-body binding formula — mind/bone, thought/sinew, insight/vein, counsel/flesh, consideration/skin (¶35) — and its systematic reversal by the Light Mind (¶38); (5) the new man's five virtues mapped to five faculties (¶40); (6) Sin's progressive rebellion through the five faculties in reverse order (¶43-49, extracted from institutional wrapping). Clear editorial fatigue: ¶44-50 embed substrate faculty-progression in institutional church-discipline narrative; ¶57-67 are entirely institutional apostolate material with exhortative closure. The substrate fatigue shift (-2.93) and institutional shift (+1.19) confirm the second half is editorially overlaid. The body-cosmos mapping and soul-body binding formula are among the most pristine substrate passages in the entire Kephalaia.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Days and the Two Deaths
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly substrate teaching. It presents a systematic cosmological classification of three great days (cosmic narrative of First Man, reign in new aeon, Father's eternal unveiling) and two deaths (mixing of light with darkness, eternal separation of sinful souls). Both sides of every mapping stay within the cosmic system throughout — no contemporary institutions, no application to the editor's world, no editorial bridge. The only editorial material is dialogue framing in ¶1-3 and ¶13. The seam flags on ¶5 and ¶12 are false positives (empty institutional vocabulary). No editorial fatigue pattern. A remarkably clean teaching chapter with a Persian-style enumeration structure.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Things that were established by the Light
chapters.note: A remarkably pure chapter. After the formulaic dialogue frame opener (P1), the entire teaching body (P2-6) is oldest-layer eschatological cosmology. The three-fold enumeration maps cosmic necessity: (1) the new luminous earth built over this earth, (2) the coffin/prison of the dark fire, (3) condemned souls crucified on the enemy. The final paragraph describes the sealing of the final lump and the permanent separation/sterilization of Darkness. Both sides of every mapping stay within the cosmic system throughout. No citations, no institutional references, no contemporary application, no exhortation. The zero substrate vocabulary score reflects the narrow vocabulary list (zoomorphic/metal/taste markers), not the actual teaching character. Significant lacunae in P3-4 obscure details of the first two cosmic necessities.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Blows that befell the Enemy because of the Light
chapters.note: This is a remarkably clean substrate chapter — a compact, numbered three-fold eschatological teaching about three cosmic blows against the Enemy/Darkness. The entire structure (first war, second dissolution, third separation) maps cosmic process onto cosmic process with no contemporary application, no institutional content, no exhortation, and no citations. The only non-substrate material is the brief dialogue frame attribution in P1. Gardner's note about 'rudimentary redaction' in ch. 39-41 may refer to the sequence ordering rather than heavy editorial overlay within the chapter itself. The exhortation that Gardner mentions (exhorting the faithful despite persecution) is not present in the surviving text as given — it may have been in a lost section or may refer to the broader chapter context not included here. The oldest teaching layer is overwhelmingly dominant.

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Vessels
chapters.note: The oldest teaching layer is strongly dominant. The chapter teaches the cosmic process of three-vessel discharge through two extended correspondential analogies (doctor/healing and mother/birth with body-layer enumeration) and a systematic twelve-deed enumeration. The analogies are structurally rich: the birth analogy maps seven body-layers (marrow, bones, tendons, flesh, veins, blood, skin) doubled through mother+child to eighteen garments — classic body-cosmos correspondence. The twelve deeds (¶14-32) are compact substrate enumeration of cosmic advantages. Editorial overlay is light: dialogue frame in ¶1-2 and ¶13, counterfactual contemporary applications in ¶16-20 (with 'today' anchors and one institutional reference to fasting in ¶19), and a closing self-reference in ¶33. The negative editorial fatigue score (-0.79) confirms the second half is cleaner than the first. Teaching purity 0.670. The seam flags on ¶17-18 are likely false positives — the bridge connectives continue a three-fold iteration (one per vessel) rather than extending to institutional content.

chapters.title: Concerning the Vessels
chapters.note: A remarkably clean teaching chapter dominated by substrate cosmological process description. The chapter describes the three-fold discharge cycle: the Father of Life pours dark vessels (water, darkness, fire) onto earth, the corresponding dark elements in the earths are drawn upward by sympathetic attraction ('like draws like'), then both are swept into prepared pits. The systematic parallel structure across paragraphs 9-11 (water, then darkness, then fire) is classic substrate enumeration. No editorial bridge, institutional, or exhortation material detected. The only later material is dialogue frame formulas in paragraphs 1, 2, 7, 8. The term 'Father of Life' for the demiurge (rather than 'Living Spirit') may preserve an earlier stratum as Gardner notes. The negative editorial fatigue score confirms the chapter stays consistently substratic throughout.

chapters.title: Concerning the Sea Giant
chapters.note: This chapter is nearly pure substrate — systematic cosmological teaching about the sea giant's formation and cosmic function. Teaching purity 0.936 is accurate. No editorial bridge, institutional, or exhortation vocabulary detected. The only non-substrate material is the single-line dialogue frame formula in paragraph 1. The teaching describes: (1) how the Living Spirit directed waste from the three vessels into the sea, explaining its salt and bitterness; (2) how the Father of Life purified the stellar sphere, casting sediment into the sea where it formed the sea giant bearing zodiacal impressions; (3) the three cosmic purposes of the sea giant — purifying the sphere, fettering the zodiac powers, and gathering all elements. Every mapping stays within the cosmic system. The craftsman analogy in paragraph 6 serves cosmic explanation, not contemporary application. This is one of the purest substrate chapters in the corpus.

chapters.title: Concerning the Vessels
chapters.note: Remarkably pure substrate chapter. Teaching purity 1.000 with zero editorial fatigue. The entire chapter follows a single systematic pattern — "Before X was discharged/born/rebelled, a place was prepared for it" — iterating through cosmic entities and their pre-prepared containment places. Both sides of every mapping stay within the cosmic-architectural system: vessels→ditches, sea giant→great sea, waste→gehennas, rebels→hostels, abortions→gathering-place, watchers→prison, giants' children→cities. No editorial bridge, institutional, or exhortation vocabulary detected anywhere. This chapter appears to preserve a nearly intact substrate teaching sequence about cosmic foreknowledge and containment architecture. The enumeration structure (each paragraph = one cosmic entity and its prepared place) is characteristic of the oldest systematic teaching layer.

chapters.title: Concerning the Ambassador
chapters.note: A highly systematic substrate teaching about cosmic pre-ordination/foreknowledge of the light. Seven moments follow a uniform pattern: 'Before [condition], [cosmic agent] was [prepared].' The structure is self-evidently complete and architectonic. Only ¶1 (dialogue frame) and ¶5 (editorial bridge inserting 'the sects' into the cosmic pattern) fall outside the oldest layer. Teaching purity is very high (0.913). The moderate institutional drift in the second half is minimal, concentrated in ¶5. The chapter preserves a remarkably intact substrate teaching about emanation sequence and cosmic determinism.

chapters.title: Concerning the Four great Things
chapters.note: An exceptionally pure substrate chapter. The entire teaching — the four-fold distribution of the ruling-power (ten firmaments, eight earths, walls/vessels, stellar sphere), the binding of cosmic leaders to the wheel, and the king-kingdom structural correspondence — stays within the cosmic system throughout. No institutional, editorial bridge, or exhortation vocabulary detected. The only editorial material is the dialogue frame opening formula in P1 and the first-person closure in P9. The seam flag on P9 is a false positive: the bridge connective 'Now, just as' returns the king analogy to cosmic application rather than bridging to institutional content. Teaching purity 0.921 is confirmed by close reading.

chapters.title: Concerning the Conduits
chapters.note: Overwhelmingly substrate chapter. The teaching describes three conduits (lihme) connecting heavenly powers to earthly domains, through which life ascends and waste descends. The entire cosmological architecture—conduits, roots, the wheel of stars, the Ambassador myth, cosmic geography—maps domain to domain without ever reaching into the contemporary world. No editorial bridge, institutional, or exhortation vocabulary detected at all. The only later material consists of thin dialogue frame formulas wrapping the teaching. The Persian dialogue tradition is strong here: the disciples' questions about zodiacal authority and conduit hierarchy reveal teaching structure. Heavy lacunae in the later paragraphs (22-24) but the surviving words are consistently cosmological.

chapters.title: Concerning the Wheel and the Conduits
chapters.note: A remarkably clean, short teaching chapter. The oldest substrate layer is overwhelmingly dominant. The only later material is minimal dialogue frame formulas in ¶1 and ¶2. No editorial bridge, no institutional content, no exhortation. The teaching is a systematic cosmological-process explanation: the conduits (extending from heavens to earths) are spiritual/pneumatic, therefore the wheel of stars passes through them without cutting or entangling — illustrated by ship-through-water and bird-through-air analogies. Both sides of every mapping stay within the cosmic/natural system. The negative editorial fatigue score (-1.54) with substrate increasing in the second half confirms the chapter is substrate-dominant throughout.

chapters.title: Concerning these Names: God, Rich One, and Angel; who they are.
chapters.note: A remarkably clean substrate chapter. The teaching is a systematic three-fold emanation hierarchy (gods, rich ones, angels) mapped across three domains: eternal archetypes, cosmic agents in the contest, and eschatological households. Both sides of every mapping stay within the cosmic system throughout. The only non-substrate material is dialogue frame attribution (¶2 fully, and frame formulas in ¶1, ¶3, ¶7, ¶10). No editorial bridge, no exhortation, no institutional extension. The seam flag on ¶10 is a false positive — the third application maps to cosmic households (Great Spirit, Beloved of the Lights, Ambassador), not to institutional structures. The order shift in the third application (god→angel→rich instead of god→rich→angel) may reflect intentional mapping to three emanation series (descent, creation, redemption). Teaching purity is high and editorial fatigue is minimal.

chapters.title: Concerning the First Man
chapters.note: Remarkably clean substrate chapter. Teaching purity 1.000 with zero editorial fatigue and zero scores for editorial_bridge, institutional, or exhortation across all paragraphs. The entire chapter (minus the one-line dialogue frame opening) is systematic cosmological teaching about the First Man's five garments (fire, wind, water, light, air) and their cosmic roles in the battle with Darkness. Both sides of every mapping stay within the cosmic system throughout. The five-element nomenclature and the process of mixture/wounding are core substrate features. The text is heavily lacunose but the teaching structure is clear.

chapters.title: Concerning the [ ... ] of the Light
chapters.note: This chapter is predominantly later editorial material — a homiletic structure using cosmological narrative (light's unity vs. darkness's disunity) as a springboard for worldly analogy and community exhortation. Teaching purity is 0.000; no systematic correspondential mapping (zoomorphic, metal, taste, five-element) is present. Heavy lacunae in paragraphs 1-2 obscure the original structure. Overall, this chapter preserves at best fragments of old cosmological teaching, heavily wrapped in editorial application.

chapters.title: Concerning the First Man
chapters.note: This chapter is almost entirely oldest teaching substrate. The only editorial element is the dialogue frame formula in ¶1. The teaching describes the First Man's descent, the construction of the universe from captured dark powers, and the devastation of the dark storehouses — using two correspondential analogies (marsh/net and body/head-limbs). The body-cosmos mapping in ¶5-6 is a recognized substrate marker. No institutional, exhortation, or editorial bridge vocabulary appears anywhere in the chapter. Despite heavy lacunae damage throughout, the cosmological process narrative is coherent and systematic.

chapters.title: [Concerning] the Quality of the Garments
chapters.note: This chapter is almost entirely oldest teaching layer. Teaching purity is 1.000 with zero editorial fatigue. The chapter describes the Living Spirit's construction of the universe from the mixture of light and darkness, using craft analogies (architect, carpenter) that belong to the ancient demiurge-as-craftsman tradition. No institutional, exhortation, or editorial_bridge vocabulary appears anywhere. The only later material is the brief dialogue frame formula in P1. The craft metaphors in P3-5, while not pure cosmos→cosmos correspondential mapping, serve the cosmological teaching and bear no marks of editorial extension — they describe HOW the cosmic builder works using timeless craft analogies rooted in ancient Near Eastern cosmological pedagogy. P4's seam flag for 'Furthermore' is overridden: content continues the same analogical teaching with no register shift to institutional material.

chapters.title: Concerning the Fashioning of Adam
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly substrate teaching with minimal editorial overlay. The oldest layer dominates: a systematic cosmological teaching about the Ambassador's image display, the rulers' unauthorized fashioning of Adam and Eve as an imperfect copy, and a three-fold enumeration of figures fashioned outside intercourse (sea giant, sea monster/Adamant, vegetation). A correspondential parable (the noble woman) is embedded as a teaching device — both sides of the mapping stay within the cosmic system. The only clearly non-substrate material is the dialogue frame attribution in ¶2, the pedagogical address formulas in ¶1/3/9, and the transitional marker in ¶8. No editorial bridge, institutional, or exhortation layers are detectable. The substrate vocabulary actually increases in the second half, consistent with the chapter-level shift data (+0.44). The term 'crucified in the totality' in ¶7 is distinctively Manichaean but describes cosmic process rather than contemporary application.

chapters.title: [Concerning Saklas and his Powers]
chapters.note: This chapter contains a strong, dominant substrate layer organized around two major teaching units: (1) the transmission of the Ambassador's image through Sin/Matter to the rulers who shaped Adam and Eve (¶1-4), and (2) the faculty-storehouse system of the body (¶6-24, 27-28), which is one of the most systematic body-cosmos correspondences in the Kephalaia. The faculty-storehouse teaching maps five senses to five faculties, each with internal storehouses and repositories, governed by the heart-faculty. This is followed by a gates/watchmen correspondence mapping body orifices to a fortified camp. The Light Mind's entry and transformation of the body's systems completes the cosmological architecture. Editorial additions are light: dialogue frame attributions (easily stripped), one pedagogical summary closure (¶5), one editorial bridge applying the transformation teaching to institutional Manichaean worship practices (¶26), and a final exhortation (¶29). The chapter shows mild editorial fatigue in ¶25-26 where worldly examples and institutional vocabulary enter the application of the faculty transformation. Gardner notes the unusual shift from 'Light Mind' to 'Holy Spirit' terminology in ¶28.

chapters.title: Concerning the Generation of Adam
chapters.note: The oldest teaching layer is the five-fold powers succession (year, month, day, hour, moment) in ¶3-6 — a systematic enumerated teaching mapping cosmic temporal authorities to generational lifespan, classic substrate. The problem statement (¶2) with its zodiac observation is also clearly old. The second half introduces a complementary light-withdrawal explanation (¶7) and a birth-mechanism teaching (¶10) whose substrate status is less certain — the editorial fatigue score (0.74) and substrate vocabulary dropping to 0.00 in the second half suggest editorial extension. Gardner confirms the two-section structure: powers explanation (144.15-146.8) followed by a 'more immediate lesson' (146.8-147.17). The chapter's low teaching purity score (0.133) reflects the absence of canonical substrate markers (zoomorphic forms, metals) rather than absence of old teaching — the five-fold powers nomenclature is differently structured.

chapters.title: The Four Powers that grieve
chapters.note: A short chapter with a clear two-layer structure. The substrate teaching (¶2-3) describes two cosmic powers—Mother of Life and First Man—grieving for their children/sons who are bound in Darkness and assaulted by enemies. This is pure cosmic-to-cosmic mapping: cosmic parent → cosmic offspring → cosmic bondage/conflict. The editorial layer (¶4-5) extends the enumeration pattern to Mani himself as 'the third one who grieves,' applying the cosmic grief template to his church community and unredeemed souls. The editorial seam at ¶4 is clean: the substrate enumeration ('The first...', 'The second...') is complete at two cosmic powers, and 'The third one who grieves am I' is Mani's self-insertion that extends the pattern to institutional content. Gardner notes the title promises four powers but only three appear, suggesting possible textual loss or compositional irregularity. The substrate portion is intact and coherent as a teaching about cosmic parental grief.

chapters.title: The Chapter of the Elements that wept
chapters.note: The oldest teaching layer is dominant. Paragraphs 2-7 form a complete, self-contained four-fold cosmological teaching about the weeping of the light elements (garments/sons of the First Man) at four stages of the cosmic drama. The enumeration structure (first, second, third, fourth) is systematic and internally complete. Both sides of every mapping stay within the cosmic system: cosmic beings weep at cosmic events. The teaching cycle closes naturally at P7 with the explanation of why the fourth weeping is worst. P8 then bridges to apostolic mission with 'Therefore, due to' — a classic editorial seam extending the completed teaching to justify apostolic suffering. P9 is a brief closing exhortation. No editorial bridge or institutional vocabulary intrudes into the core teaching sequence. No NT citations detected. Negative editorial fatigue score (-0.52) is consistent with the editorial material being brief and confined to the end.

chapters.title: Concerning the Four Fathers; what they are like.
chapters.note: A remarkably pure body-cosmos correspondence teaching with minimal editorial overlay. The four-fold mapping (directive→Father, eyes→light ships, body→living soul, tongue→Jesus the Splendour) is systematic and complete. Both sides of every mapping stay within the cosmic system throughout. The only editorial material is the dialogue frame opening (¶1 attribution) and closing (¶9). The negative editorial fatigue score confirms substrate dominance increasing toward the chapter's end. 'Jesus the Splendour' functions as a cosmic emanation entity (the revealer principle) rather than a historical figure; the name may overlay an older cosmic revealer figure from the Persian tradition. The teaching structure itself—mapping four cosmic powers to four body faculties—is characteristic of the oldest correspondential substrate.

chapters.title: Concerning the Garment of the Waters: how great is its Measure.
chapters.note: This chapter is dominated by a biographical narrative frame (Mani visiting King Shapur, standing on the Tigris quay during flood). The oldest teaching layer — about the First Man assuming elemental garments, the cosmic rulers consuming vast waters, the binding of the mighty giants, and the eschatological dissolution of the material universe — is embedded within this narrative but extractable. The substrate teaching about the measure of the garment of waters is genuine cosmological-correspondential material about cosmic scale and elemental combat. The Tigris flood serves as a pedagogical occasion that the compilers used to frame this teaching. Gardner's note that the chapter's value lies in 'historical reference' confirms that the narrative frame is the editors' contribution. Paragraph 9 is the purest substrate passage. The chapter lacks the systematic zoomorphic/metal/taste mappings seen in Ch. 6 but preserves cosmic process vocabulary (elements, garments, rulers, binding, dissolution).

chapters.title: Concerning the Three Rocks
chapters.note: A compact three-fold cosmological teaching about modes of absolute stability ('rocks') established in the cosmic structure. The oldest teaching layer is dominant: a thesis paragraph, three enumerated items, and a summary recapitulation. The only significant editorial intrusion is in ¶5, where the third rock's cosmic placement has been replaced with 'the holy church' — an institutional substitution visible by comparison with ¶3's cosmic location ('this zone') and ¶6's summary ('three great places of these selfsame worlds'). The chapter otherwise preserves clean substrate with systematic emanation and placement patterns.

chapters.title: Concerning Love
chapters.note: Short binary teaching (Love/Hate) with a clear editorial insertion at ¶3. The substrate teaching maps Love → Father of Greatness and Hate → first death/land of Darkness. The editor extends the Love mapping to the holy church and apostle, mimicking the 'single body' pattern from ¶2 and adding an NT citation (John 15:13). The Hate sequence (¶4-5) remains substantially intact as cosmological substrate, with ¶5's 'today' language describing the ongoing cosmic middle-time rather than pointing at specific contemporary institutions. The seam flag on ¶4 is a false positive (zero institutional vocabulary, purely cosmological content). The derivation chain at the end of ¶5 ('the hated from the hated; the envy from the envy') is a distinctive substrate formula mapping ontological origin.

chapters.title: [Concerning Adam]
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly oldest-layer substrate. The teaching is highly systematic: a three-fold enumeration of Adam's cosmic preeminence (image, soul-structure, cosmic seal) followed by a seven-fold enumeration of the rulers' purposes in creating Adam. Every mapping stays within the cosmic system — no paragraph reaches into contemporary institutions, social structures, or religious practices. The only non-substrate material is the dialogue frame opening (¶1) and a brief editorial bridge phrase in ¶6. The body-cosmos correspondence (zodiac sealed in Adam), the elemental distribution teaching, and the seal-ring metaphor are all classic substrate features. Negative editorial fatigue score confirms no drift toward later layers. This is one of the purest teaching chapters in the corpus.

chapters.title: Concerning the Sun
chapters.note: Substantial substrate teaching organized in three systematic sections: (1) seven goods of the sun contrasted with seven evils of the night (¶5-11, ¶14-20), (2) five archetypes of the sun (¶23-27), (3) three qualities corresponding to the mystery of the Father (¶30-32). The oldest teaching layer is dominant. Editorial bridges are interspersed at section transitions (¶3, ¶12, ¶21, ¶33) polemicizing against 'the sects' for not recognizing these cosmic mysteries. The chapter closes with a Gospel of Thomas citation (¶36) and classic exhortation/beatitude closure (¶37-38), confirming the editorial fatigue pattern flagged by the computational analysis. Low substrate vocabulary scores throughout reflect the absence of this chapter's key terms (sun, night, light, darkness) from the substrate marker list (which targets zoomorphic/metal/taste correspondences), NOT the absence of substrate content. The 7+7+5+3 enumeration structure is the teaching's skeleton. Gardner/McBride's suggestion of heliolatry native to Egyptian Manichaeism may be true at the compilation level, but the correspondential structure (sun as sign of the light-realm, night as sign of Darkness) belongs to the older substrate layer.

chapters.title: Concerning the Ambassador
chapters.note: Clean chapter structure: dialogue frame (¶1) → substrate teaching (¶2-6) → exhortation (¶7) → dialogue frame closure (¶8). The substrate core is a tightly structured cosmological correspondence teaching mapping two daily solar phenomena (sunrise/sunset) onto two terminal cosmic events (First Man's descent into Darkness / Last Statue's final ascent). Both sides of every mapping remain within the cosmic system. The teaching uses the natural solar cycle as a correspondential key to the entire cosmic drama — the 'second time' of mixture is the daylight between two eternal nights. The exhortation in ¶7 is a clear later addition applying the teaching to pastoral urgency. No editorial bridge material detected. The substrate dominates this chapter.

chapters.title: Concerning the Light-Giver
chapters.note: This chapter contains no detectable substrate material. Teaching purity is 0.000. The entire chapter is built around a personal analogy — Mani comparing himself to the sun — which is apostolic/institutional self-identification, not systematic cosmological-correspondential teaching. The sun's behavior (rays extending and withdrawing) serves as a natural analogy for Mani's mission, not as a correspondential map of cosmic domains. No five-fold structures, no zoomorphic-realm mappings, no metal-body or taste-world chains. The chapter is cleanly layered: dialogue frame (¶1), institutional apostolic narrative (¶2-3), and exhortation (¶4). Gardner's synopsis confirms the chapter plays on the title 'enlightener' applied to both the sun and Mani — a hagiographic identification, not a substrate teaching.

chapters.title: Concerning Fire
chapters.note: A very clean, compact substrate chapter. Five-fold systematic classification of fire's works — consistent with the oldest teaching layer's approach of mapping natural/cosmic processes through numbered enumerations. Paragraph 3's four-fold separation of wood (fire, light, ash, smoke) is distinctly correspondential, mapping fire's action as element-separator. No editorial bridge, no institutional content, no exhortation. The only non-substrate material is the brief dialogue frame attribution in ¶1. NLP scores all read 0.0, likely because the chapter uses basic natural vocabulary (fire, wood, light, ash) that doesn't trigger the curated diagnostic term lists — but the substrate quality is structural (five-fold enumeration, systematic classification) rather than lexical.

chapters.title: Concerning the Twelve Signs of the Zodiac and the Five Stars
chapters.note: Extremely high substrate purity. The chapter contains systematic cosmological-correspondential teaching mapping zodiac signs and planets to the five worlds of darkness, then mapping zodiac triplicities to four cosmic domains of affliction. Both mappings stay entirely within the cosmic system — no contemporary application, no institutional content, no exhortation. The editorial layer is limited to dialogue frame formulas (opening/attribution) and first-person recap framing in ¶10-13. The seam flags on ¶3 and ¶10 are false positives — both paragraphs contain pure cosmos→cosmos mappings with zero institutional content. Gardner notes the structural tension of fitting twelve into pentads and reconciling the seven rulers with Mani's system; these tensions are visible in the teaching itself (uneven 2-2-3-3-2 distribution) and represent genuine substratic difficulty, not editorial confusion. The negative editorial fatigue score confirms the substrate runs strong throughout.

chapters.title: Concerning the Body: It was constructed after the Pattern of the Universe
chapters.note: Overwhelmingly substrate chapter — the oldest body-cosmos correspondence teaching dominates. Teaching purity 0.967 with no editorial bridge, no exhortation, and negligible editorial fatigue. Gardner notes redaction from multiple sources/lessons, visible in the distinct teaching blocks: (1) body→cosmic structures (¶2-3), (2) five watches and their conflicts (¶5-16), (3) five body regions→cosmic rulers with ethical framing (¶17-24), (4) four body worlds with seven rulers each (¶25-29), (5) zodiac-body correspondences in two schemas (¶31-36), (6) numerical powers in the body (¶38-39). The ethical framing in ¶18-22 ('Whoever will master X resembles cosmic ruler Y') is the main editorial overlay — it wraps substrate body-cosmos mappings in application to the elect. The three dialogue frame paragraphs are minimal. This chapter preserves some of the most systematic body-cosmos correspondence teaching in the Kephalaia.

chapters.title: Concerning the Gathering in of the [E]lements
chapters.note: A very short chapter with a remarkably clean substrate core. Paragraph 2 is the heart: a systematic degree-based return sequence mapping the gathering-in of the five light elements upward through cosmic intermediaries to the aeons. This is pure correspondential substrate — an ascending chain where each domain gathers into the next. Both sides of every mapping stay within the cosmic system. The chapter shows mild editorial fatigue: the brief devotional closure in P3 ('place of rest for ever and ever') is appended after the teaching is complete. The substrate teaching in P2 is notable for its restoration brackets, indicating manuscript damage that has been editorially restored — the Pillar→First Man→Ambassador chain is reconstructed.

chapters.title: Concerning the worn and torn apart Garments, or the tattered Clothes, or the Elements, the Cross, and the rest too
chapters.note: A remarkably clean teaching chapter. The substrate dominates: a systematic terminological exposition mapping seven names for the devoured light to their cosmic referents. No editorial bridge material, no exhortation, no institutional content. The editorial layer is confined entirely to the dialogue frame (¶1, 4, 5, 6) and minor framing phrases in ¶2, 3, 7. The teaching structure is: (1) enumerate terms as questions, (2) define each term by mapping name→cosmic entity/condition, (3) conclude with restoration theology. chapters.title: Concerning the Envy of Matter
chapters.note: The oldest teaching layer is a compact cosmological narrative about Matter's envy expressed through three cosmic episodes: the First Man, the Ambassador's image, and Adam. This substrate is clearly bounded — paragraphs 2-4 are pure cosmological narrative with both sides of every mapping internal to the cosmic system. The editors extended the three-fold enumeration to a fourth item (Christ and the apostles), then to Mani and his church, then to practical community warnings, then to exhortation. The editorial fatigue pattern is textbook: institutional vocabulary jumps from 0.0 to 8.30 in the second half. Teaching purity is very low (0.109), reflecting that the substrate core is small and the editorial extension substantial.

chapters.title: Concerning the living Fire: It is present in Eight Places.
chapters.note: Exceptionally clean substrate chapter. A systematic eight-fold enumeration mapping the living fire (one of the five light elements) to eight cosmic locations, with the fire identified as 'consideration' (one of the five intellectual faculties). Both sides of every mapping stay within the cosmic system — land of light, the Father, the First Man's armour, the ship of the day, the light-giver of the night, the Living Spirit's body, the new earth, eschatological revelation. No editorial bridge, institutional, or exhortation material detected. The only non-substrate material is the opening dialogue frame formula. Heavy lacunae in several paragraphs but the teaching structure is intact.

chapters.title: [Concerning the Letter (?)]
chapters.note: A compact chapter with a clear two-part structure. ¶2-3 form a complete cosmological teaching pair: the summons (call) as a cosmic letter from Living Spirit to First Man, and the obedience (answer) as a cosmic letter from First Man to Living Spirit. Both cosmic beings and the letter metaphor stay entirely within the cosmic system. ¶4-6 then extend this 'letter' pattern to the institutional church — Light Mind as letter to the holy church, good works as letter to Christ. The editorial seam is sharp: the word 'also/too' in ¶4 explicitly extends the cosmic list, but the target is now the editor's community. Editorial fatigue data strongly confirms: substrate 12.50→0.98, institutional 0.00→16.09. The oldest teaching layer is the primordial call-and-answer narrative, which maps the summons and obedience as cosmic communications containing all foreknowledge.

chapters.title: [Conce]rning Lord Manichaios: how he journeyed.
chapters.note: This chapter contains zero substrate cosmological-correspondential teaching. Teaching purity is 0.000. The entire chapter is apostolic narrative — Mani's missionary journeys through India, Persia, Mesene, Babylon, and Media/Parthia, his repeated summons by King Shapur, and opposition from authorities in various lands. It includes a near-verbatim NT citation (John 3:19-20) repeated twice (¶7, ¶11). The chapter is framed by a disciple's request for 'two Manis' and closes with exhortation (¶25) and devotional response (¶26). This is purely institutional material — biographical, hagiographic, and historically situated — with no cosmic mappings, no correspondential architecture, and no trace of the oldest teaching layer.

chapters.title: The Chapter of the Four Kingdoms
chapters.note: This chapter contains NO cosmological-correspondential substrate. Teaching purity is 0.000. The editorial fatigue pattern is strong: substrate is front-loaded (first half 6.47), institutional accumulates in the second half (7.56). Teaching purity 0.392 reflects the heavy institutional overlay.

chapters.title: Concerning why if a [Nail] is cut the Person shall not be sick; but if a Limb is cut he shall immediately be pained.
chapters.note: Heavily lacunose chapter preserving a body-cosmos correspondence teaching: body↔earth, limbs↔trees, varieties of trees↔varieties of body parts (some regrow when cut, others do not). This is systematic body-cosmos mapping consistent with the substrate pattern identified in Ch.70. The teaching purity score of 0.0 is misleading — the substrate vocabulary here uses common terms (body, earth, trees) rather than the marked zoomorphic/metal terms the pipeline detects. The STRUCTURE is pure correspondential mapping: both sides stay within the natural/cosmic system. Dialogue frame is dominant by paragraph count (5 of 7) but the two teaching paragraphs contain the bulk of the word count. No editorial bridge, institutional, or exhortation layers detected — this chapter appears to be substrate teaching wrapped in dialogue frame with no later editorial extension.

chapters.title: Concerning why Some shall delay to come forth from the Body, and Others die in an instant.
chapters.note: Extremely fragmentary chapter with extensive lacunae. The topic — why some souls are released quickly from the body while others delay — points to cosmological process teaching about soul-body separation mechanics. Paragraph 2 preserves enumeration structure ('[sec]ond') suggesting a systematic numbered teaching about categories of soul release, but almost all content is lost. Gardner notes the chapter likely continued onto a now-destroyed leaf. The substrate teaching that survives is skeletal but identifiable by its impersonal, process-oriented voice and enumeration structure. Almost entirely destroyed chapter. Gardner confirms that only a few words can be read and no overall sense of contents is achievable. No editorial, institutional, exhortation, or dialogue frame markers are detectable in the surviving fragments. All register scores are 0.0. Preserved as potential substrate solely because the few readable words lean cosmological — this classification carries minimal confidence.

The chapter preserves a three-name cosmological teaching about the First Man ('approved', 'righteous', 'only begotten') in ¶3–5, which is genuine substrate — systematic, impersonal explanation of cosmic epithets with both mapping sides staying within the cosmic system (aeons of light, the enemy, the Father, five sons). The editorial layer then applies these cosmic attributes to the community (¶6, ¶9–10), with ¶4 showing institutional vocabulary ('catechumen') inserted into substrate teaching. Heavy lacunae throughout limit confidence. Gardner's synopsis confirms the Christological/exhortative editorial purpose. Moderate editorial fatigue with exhortation surging in the second half.

chapters.title: Concerning the Two Essences
chapters.note: This chapter is overwhelmingly polemical, not expository. The title names a substrate topic (the two essences = primordial duality) but the chapter uses that topic as a weapon against monotheism rather than systematically mapping it. Mani is preaching/arguing, not teaching cosmological correspondences. The only substrate fragment is the brief naming of the two essences and their paired opposites in the opening paragraph. The remainder is direct argumentative address ('you'), rhetorical catalogues of evil, citations of Jesus's tree parable as proof-text, and eschatological warnings. Teaching purity 0.000 confirms this. No systematic mapping (face→realm, metal→body, taste→world) appears anywhere. The five trees are mentioned in ¶6 but as citation within polemic, not as expounded teaching. Heavy lacunae throughout make the chapter additionally fragmentary.

chapters.title: Concerning the Sect of the Basket
chapters.note: Chapter has a clear two-part structure: (1) paragraphs 1-4 are a narrative encounter with a presbyter from a non-Manichaean sect, entirely institutional/editorial/exhortatory material including polemic and a beatitude identification of 'basket' with 'holy church'; (2) paragraphs 5-6 contain heavily fragmentary but recognizable cosmological teaching — cosmic architecture (pillars, disk, sea), cosmic beings (Mind, Youth, Porter, five sons of the Man, Adamant of Light), and cosmic enumerations (thirty-six, twenty-two, twelve, seven, four). The substrate is NOT dominant — it survives only in the latter, very damaged portion. Teaching purity is low (0.254). The editorial fatigue pattern is inverted here — substrate increases in the second half (+5.39), suggesting the cosmological teaching was appended or preserved at the end while the first half was fully replaced by narrative polemic. Gardner's uncertainty about the chapter's coherence is justified — the connection between the sect discussion and the cosmological catalogue is unclear.

chapters.title: Concerning the 'Assent' and the 'Amen'
chapters.note: This chapter is predominantly institutional/editorial material explaining the cosmic significance of Manichaean liturgical practices (assent and amen). The substrate core is limited to ¶2-4: a compact teaching that maps assent→summons and amen→obedience (answer), then describes how these cosmic entities functioned as portals for the First Man's redemption and as purifiers of the living soul. From ¶5 onward, the teaching applies these cosmic archetypes to congregational worship practice — describing liturgical sealing, the formation of ascending images from collective sound, healing power, and overcoming temptation. All of this later material has one side of its mapping reaching into institutional practice ('the congregation', 'great crowds of people', 'the elect', 'their alms'). The text is heavily damaged throughout with extensive lacunae, especially ¶4 and ¶10-16. Substrate vocabulary is entirely concentrated in the first half (8.71→0.00), confirming the core teaching ends early. Gardner notes this chapter was completed from Funk's working text beyond the published edition.
